checks.heading: Checks
start.heading: Start a sign-in
then.heading: Then
result.notOk: Not every check passed. Each one below says which, and why — a single verdict for the whole response would say “it failed” and nothing anybody could act on.
wsfed.heading: Mock relying party
wsfed.sub: NON-SPEC. A relying party is not part of an identity provider — this one exists so the passive requestor profile can be exercised, and verified, without a second service.
wsfed.realm: Its realm is {realm}, and it is also the default wreply: a sign-in request that names no return address is POSTed here.
wsfed.request.saml11Note: — the default, and what AD FS issues.
wsfed.request.trust13: SAML 1.1 in a ws-sx 200512 RSTR Collection
wsfed.request.trust13Note: — the other wrapper a relying party may be given.
wsfed.request.wfreshNote: — forces the sign-in screen even when a session already exists.
wsfed.request.multifactorNote: — a session with one factor (a passwordless key included) is sent to sign in again with a second factor required, and the assertion says multipleauthn only once there really were two.
wsfed.request.hardwareNote: — a session that used no security key is sent to sign in again, and refused if it still used none.
wsfed.signOutNote: — ends the session and sends a cleanup request to every relying party it signed into.
wsfed.metadataNote: this relying party would be configured from.
wsfed.wctx: wctx for this attempt: {wctx}. It is checked on the way back, because an identity provider that decoded and re-encoded it produces the same symptom as a lost session.
wsfed.result.heading: Sign-in response received
wsfed.result.sub: Mock relying party at {realm} — POSTed to, not redirected to, which is the whole shape of this profile.
wsfed.result.keepsNothing: This relying party keeps no session. It verifies what it was sent and shows it, which is all a mock relying party can honestly claim to do.
saml2.title.unresolved: Artifact did not resolve — mock service provider
saml2.heading: Mock service provider
saml2.sub: NON-SPEC. A service provider is not part of an identity provider — this one exists so the Web Browser SSO profile can be exercised, and verified, without a second service.
saml2.entity: Its entityID is {entityId}, and it is also the default AssertionConsumerServiceURL: an AuthnRequest that names none is answered here.
saml2.requestUnsigned: Response over {binding}, from an UNSIGNED request
saml2.requestSigned: — the request goes on the Redirect binding, signed, and ProtocolBinding asks for the answer on {binding}.
saml2.requestNotSigned: — the request goes on the Redirect binding with no signature, and ProtocolBinding asks for the answer on {binding}.
saml2.artifactNote: The browser will carry a SAMLart back here and this page resolves it.
saml2.refused: This realm requires signed requests, so it is REFUSED.
saml2.answered: This realm accepts unsigned requests, so it is answered.
saml2.sloNote: — ends the session and names every service provider it signed into.
saml2.metadata: This service provider’s own identity provider metadata
saml2.metadataNote: — a distinct entityID and its own endpoints, which is what makes the metadata unique per application.
saml2.signedNote: The first three AuthnRequests are SIGNED on the Redirect binding’s query string (section 3.4.4.1) with this service’s own key, and the Single Sign-On service VERIFIES them — the one entityID it trusts that key for is this page’s. The fourth is unsigned, and whether it is answered is saml2.requireSignedAuthnRequests: off in development, on in product.
saml2.result.heading: Response received
saml2.result.sub.post: Mock service provider at {entityId} — in the body of a form POST (the HTTP POST binding).
saml2.result.sub.redirect: Mock service provider at {entityId} — on the query string (the HTTP Redirect binding).
saml2.result.sub.artifact: Mock service provider at {entityId} — as a SAMLart the browser carried, resolved over the back channel.
saml2.result.ok: Every check passed. An assertion for {subject}.
saml2.result.name: Name
saml2.result.custom: The SAML 2.0 set is appended by the same assertion builder that serves WS-Trust and WS-Federation, so anything configured as a custom SAML attribute is in this table too, with no wiring of its own:
saml2.result.keepsNothing: This service provider keeps no session. It verifies what it was sent and shows it, which is all a mock service provider can honestly claim to do.
saml2.result.inProcess: The artifact was resolved IN PROCESS rather than by this service making a SOAP call to itself over HTTP — there is nothing to learn from that, and an outbound request to a URL this service computed is the shape of thing every other module here declines to make. A real service provider POSTs a signed ArtifactResolve to {ars}.
saml2.result.arsPage: The curl for it is on that endpoint’s own page.
saml2.unresolved.heading: The artifact did not resolve
saml2.unresolved.note: The commonest cause is the most interesting one: an artifact is resolvable EXACTLY ONCE (section 3.6.4.1), so loading this page again after a successful resolution lands here. That is the behaviour rather than a fault.
saml11.heading: SAML 1.1 — mock relying party
saml11.sub: A service provider that lives here, so the profile can be exercised without standing up a second one
saml11.intro: This page starts a real flow at the inter-site transfer service and then verifies what comes back, check by check. It identifies itself as {providerId} with Shibboleth’s providerId parameter, which is the only way a SAML 1.1 relying party can name itself.
saml11.transferPage: The inter-site transfer service’s own page says more.
saml11.postNote: Browser/POST (section 4.2): the whole signed assertion arrives here in a self-submitting form. Watch the intermediate page — it carries a real button, because this service sets script-src 'none' everywhere and the auto-submit is one named script.
saml11.artifactNote: Browser/Artifact (section 4.1): a 42-byte reference arrives on a redirect and this page fetches the assertion from the SAML responder over SOAP. The assertion never passes through the browser, and the artifact is destroyed by being resolved — load the result page again and the second attempt is refused.
saml11.result.noSubjectPost: No subject was found in the response.
saml11.result.noSubjectArtifact: No subject was found in the assertion.
saml11.result.target: TARGET came back as {target} — the relying party’s own state, echoed byte for byte.
saml11.result.artifactWas: The artifact was {artifact} — 42 bytes, type 0x0001: a two-byte type code, a twenty-byte SourceID that is the SHA-1 of the identity provider’s providerID, and a twenty-byte handle. The assertion never passed through this browser; it was fetched from the SAML responder.
saml11.reload: Load it again — the artifact is spent
saml11.spent.err: That artifact did not resolve: it was never issued here, it has expired, or — most likely if you just loaded this page again — it has ALREADY BEEN RESOLVED. An artifact is one-shot (saml-bindings-1.1 section 3.2.3), and resolving it destroys it.
saml11.spent.note: That is the behaviour worth seeing: a relying party that retries a resolution, or that resolves the same artifact on two workers, gets exactly this and nothing in the happy path would have shown it.
